subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Hindsight Bias
description: Learn The Hindsight Bias in one minute.

hook.text: After a stock market crash, everyone says they saw it coming. Before the crash, nobody sold.

buildup.text: Fischhoff showed that people, after learning an outcome, believe they predicted it all along.

discovery.text: Hindsight bias: knowing the result makes it feel obvious. We rewrite our past predictions.

twist.text: This bias blocks learning. If you 'knew it all along,' why would you study what went wrong?

climax.text: Record your predictions before outcomes arrive. The gap between them reveals the bias.

punchline.text: Hindsight feels like foresight. It isn't.

quiz.question: Why does hindsight bias block learning?
options: It makes us forget past events
It makes outcomes feel obvious so we don't analyze them

details.summary: Hindsight bias is the tendency to believe, after learning an outcome, that you knew it all along. Events that seemed uncertain become obvious in retrospect, making people overconfident in their predictive abilities and unfairly judgmental of past decisions.
details.whyItMatters: Hindsight bias corrupts learning from experience by making past successes seem inevitable and past failures seem obviously avoidable. It distorts accountability, preventing organizations from accurately evaluating decision quality versus luck.
takeaways: After learning outcomes, people believe they were predictable all along
Hindsight bias prevents accurate learning from both successes and failures
Decision quality should be evaluated based on information available at the time

faq.question: How does hindsight bias affect organizational learning?
faq.answer: It makes organizations punish bad outcomes even when decisions were reasonable and reward good outcomes from lucky gambles. This encourages result-oriented thinking instead of process-oriented thinking, degrading long-term decision quality.

faq.question: How can hindsight bias be reduced?
faq.answer: Record your predictions and reasoning before outcomes are known. Review decisions based on what was known at the time, not what happened. Consider alternative outcomes that could have occurred. Pre-mortems conducted before projects start also help.
